title: Scaphoid Fracture
case: Presentation (from the chapter): Radial wrist pain after a fall, sometimes mild, so the patient may think it is a sprain. Ask about the mechanism (fall on an extended wrist), timing, and whether X-rays were taken.
qa: Why can a normal X-ray mislead? Scaphoid fractures may not be visible initially.
Why are proximal fractures risky? The blood supply enters distally, so the proximal fragment may lose its supply.
Name three clinical tests. Snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness, thumb axial compression.
What do you do if tests are positive but X-ray is normal? Splint and refer for further imaging.
What is the main long-term complication? Non-union and avascular necrosis, leading to arthritis.
manualNotes: Immobilisation can be long (often 6 to 12 weeks or more depending on site). During immobilisation, keep the fingers, elbow and shoulder moving. After union: active wrist range, carpal mobilisation, grip and weight-bearing progression, sport-specific loading (push-ups, falls training). Return to contact sport only with surgeon approval.
